 Home health The sun doesn't know it's winter: Why sunscreen is essential year-round
 Dr Mukta Sachdev explains why winter doesn't mean you can skip protection from the sun's harmful UV rays Dr Mukta Sachdev Last Updated : 21 November 2026, 06:05 IST Story continues below. Go Ad Lite Join Us Prefer Comments Winter sunshine may feel gentle, but your skin still needs protection from UV rays. 
 Credit: iStock Photo
 It’s common to hear, “Doctor, I stopped using sunscreen because there isn’t much sunlight”, during the winter months. Cooler weather makes sunlight feel less intense, but your skin does not interpret sunshine quite the way you do.
 The sun does not take a holiday 
UVB contributes to sunburn, while UVA contributes to pigmentation and premature ageing. Seasonal UV levels vary, but UVA remains relevant throughout the year and can pass through ordinary window glass.
Melanin provides some natural protection, but it does not make your skin immune to sun damage. Melasma, uneven skin tone, and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation can persist throughout the year. Visible light can also worsen pigmentation in susceptible individuals.
 Choosing sunscreen 
Select a broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher. In winter, a moisturising formula may be more comfortable. People with melasma may benefit from tinted sunscreen containing iron oxides.
 How much is enough?
Apply a generous, even layer to exposed skin, including the ears, neck, and hands. Reapply every two hours during prolonged outdoor exposure and after swimming or heavy sweating. Indoor needs depend on sunlight exposure, especially when sitting near windows.
 ANYTIME, ANYWHERE.

 Can moisturiser replace sunscreen? 
Only if it is specifically labelled as offering adequate SPF and broad-spectrum protection. Otherwise, moisturiser and sunscreen serve different purposes. A moisturising sunscreen can conveniently provide both.
Sunscreen is preventive healthcare, not merely a cosmetic step. It helps reduce photoageing, pigmentation problems, and the risk of skin cancer. Enjoy the winter sunshine, but remember — cooler temperatures do not necessarily mean less ultraviolet exposure.
 (The author is a consultant dermatologist)
